qs.q: A 40‑year‑old woman tests positive for Chlamydia trachomatis and has cervical friability. What is the most appropriate partner management?
o: Treat current sexual partners per local guidelines
Treat partners only if they develop symptoms
Advise partners to be tested later
qs.e: Current sexual partners should be treated to prevent reinfection. Delaying treatment or testing only after symptoms appear increases transmission risk.
qs.s: Vaginal Discharge and Vulvovaginal Infections: Clinical Assessment,: MCQs

qs.q: Approximately what percentage of infected women are estimated to have no symptoms at all when infected with Chlamydia trachomatis?
qs.e: Chlamydia is known as a silent disease because about 70% of infected women and 50% of infected men experience no symptoms at all. The other figures listed do not correspond to the asymptomatic rate in women.

qs.q: Which diagnostic test is considered the most sensitive method available for detecting Chlamydia trachomatis genetic material?
qs.e: Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) find the DNA of Chlamydia bacteria and are the most sensitive tests available with minimal risk of false negatives. Cell culture and EIA are either less sensitive, more expensive, or slower.

qs.q: A 22-year-old woman is evaluated for contact with a partner recently diagnosed with a Chlamydia trachomatis infection. What is the typical incubation period for this bacterial pathogen?
qs.e: The incubation period for Chlamydia trachomatis is typically between 7 and 21 days. An interval of 1 to 2 days is far too short and is instead characteristic of acute bacterial gonococcal infections.

qs.q: Ophthalmia neonatorum is a form of neonatal conjunctivitis that can be acquired during birth from mothers infected with Chlamydia trachomatis and which other pathogen?
qs.e: Ophthalmia neonatorum is caused by vertical transmission of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis during passage through an infected birth canal. Both agents can cause severe conjunctivitis and potential corneal blindness if left untreated.

qs.q: A child presents with pink eye disease (trachoma/infection) linked to Chlamydia trachomatis. Which mechanical vector is noted for carrying this agent?
qs.e: Musca species (flies) transmit Chlamydia trachomatis causing pink eye disease. Blatta orientalis transmits Vibrio cholerae.
qs.s: Medical Entomology: High-Yield Tables and Key Facts: MCQs

qs.q: A group of subjects is found to have Chlamydia trachomatis infection. Which of the following laboratory methods is most likely to be useful in diagnosis of C. trachomatis?
o: Cytologic smear preparation of the affected tissue
Histological analysis of a tissue biopsy specimen
Darkfield microscopic examination of exudate or secretions
Enzyme immunoassay detection of specific antigens
qs.e: This is the easiest and most cost-effective method, since C. trachomatis cannot be easily cultured by routine methods.

qs.q: Ophthalmia neonatorum, a severe conjunctivitis, is associated with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, which are sexually transmitted infections.
o: Treponema pallidum and Herpes simplex virus
Human immunodeficiency virus and Hepatitis B virus
qs.e: Ophthalmia neonatorum is a serious eye infection in newborns. The most common causes are Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, both of which are sexually transmitted infections acquired during passage through the birth canal.

ai.title: Chlamydia trachomatis
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: A common sexually transmitted bacterium that infects the urogenital tract, causing urethritis, PID and neonatal conjunctivitis. Diagnosis relies on NAAT; treatment is doxycycline or azithromycin. Early detection prevents long‑term sequelae.

sections.p: Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular, cell‑wall‑free bacterium that spreads through sexual contact. In East Africa it is the leading cause of urethritis and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) in young adults.
It has a biphasic life cycle: elementary bodies (infectious) and reticulate bodies (replicative). It evades immunity by intracellular residence and antigenic variation.
b: No cell wall – no beta‑lactam activity

sections.p: Spread by unprotected vaginal, anal or oral sex. In the host, elementary bodies enter epithelial cells, convert to reticulate bodies, replicate, then reform elementary bodies that exit to infect new cells.
b: Can persist for months if untreated

sections.p: In men: urethritis with dysuria, mucopurulent discharge. In women: cervicitis, PID, ectopic pregnancy risk. Neonates: conjunctivitis, pneumonia.
b: PID severity graded by CDC: mild, moderate, severe

sections.p: NAAT on urine or endocervical swab is gold standard. In low‑resource settings, rapid antigen tests are available but less sensitive.

t.b: Detects Chlamydia DNA – positive means active infection
Quick screening – negative may miss infection; confirm with NAAT if available
Treats all stages; avoids resistance seen with azithromycin
Convenient single dose; useful where adherence is poor

sections.p: Remember: asymptomatic in 70% of women; PID can present with lower abdominal pain and cervical motion tenderness. In resource‑poor settings, treat empirically if high suspicion and NAAT unavailable.
b: Look for cervical motion tenderness (Chandelier sign)

sections.p: Gonorrhoea (both cause urethritis) but gonorrhoea responds to ceftriaxone; Chlamydia is resistant to beta‑lactams.
False negatives in early infection; antigen tests less sensitive; culture requires specialised media not available locally.
If severe PID (fever >38.5°C, rebound tenderness, vomiting) admit for IV antibiotics and monitor for sepsis.
Repeat NAAT 3 months after treatment to confirm cure; counsel on safe sex practices.
Screen all pregnant women and high‑risk groups; treat neonates with erythromycin eye drops to prevent blindness.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with fever, vomiting, or signs of sepsis; infertility concerns; neonatal eye discharge

faq.q: Why is Chlamydia often asymptomatic in women?
faq.a: Its intracellular life cycle evades immune detection, leading to mild or no symptoms.
Yes, untreated PID damages fallopian tubes, increasing ectopic pregnancy risk.

faq.q: Is a single dose of azithromycin effective?
faq.a: It is effective for most infections but resistance is rising; doxycycline is preferred where adherence is reliable.

exam: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with lower abdominal pain and cervical motion tenderness. What is the next best step? — Perform a cervical swab for NAAT; start empiric doxycycline and ceftriaxone if PID is suspected.
A neonate has red, watery eyes at birth. What prophylaxis should be given? — Apply erythromycin ophthalmic ointment immediately.
A patient on doxycycline develops a rash. What is the likely cause? — Drug‑induced hypersensitivity; discontinue doxycycline and switch to azithromycin.
A 30‑year‑old man has urethral discharge but negative Gram stain. What is the most likely organism? — Chlamydia trachomatis; confirm with NAAT.
